# MathBeast

**An LLM that can't lie about maths. Problems are generated by code, answers are
verified by code, and the model only explains.**

> The real guarantee, stated narrowly: it cannot lie about *the answer*, and
> every method claim in its explanation is machine-checked against verified
> steps. See [Why the guarantee is narrower than the tagline](#why-the-guarantee-is-narrower-than-the-tagline).

A verified maths engine. Pack #1 is Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics **0580** —
49 skills, 39 Core and 10 Extended.

## Try it in sixty seconds

No model required. No API key. No account.

```bash
pip install mathbeast

mathbeast drill                    # practice, engine only, no LLM anywhere
mathbeast explain pythagoras       # see the verified working
mathbeast coverage                 # what the pack covers
```

## The benchmark

**Not yet measured.** This is the number the project is really about, and it
does not exist yet, so this section is not going to pretend otherwise.

The measurement is **unsupported-claim rate**: given a model that produces a
correct final answer, how often does its explanation assert something the
engine never verified? A model can reach the right answer by a route that does
not exist. That is the failure this project exists to catch, and as far as I
know nobody has published a number for it.

```bash
mathbeast bench                    # reports the offline floor: always 0.0
mathbeast bench --model qwen2.5:3b # needs Ollama running
```

The floor is trivially zero and is not the interesting number. The comparison
worth publishing is raw small model vs chain-of-thought vs verified narration,
on a held-out set, for answer correctness, explanation correctness,
unsupported-claim rate and latency. When it exists it goes here, whatever it
shows.

## Three primitives

| | What it is | Uses an LLM? |
|---|---|---|
| **Skill** | A YAML file stating a question and an audited transform | No |
| **Checker** | Form-aware SymPy equivalence returning one of four states | No |
| **Narrator** | Explains steps the engine already verified | Yes, and only here |

A skill never states an answer. It states the expression and names a transform,
and the engine computes the answer:

```yaml
answer: "({v} + {p})({v} + {q})"
transform: expand
```

There is no answer in the file to get wrong.

### Four states, not two

SymPy's `simplify` can hang, and it returns `False` for expressions that are
true but unprovable. A boolean checker lies in both directions, so:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `PROVEN_EQUAL` | equivalence proved |
| `PROVEN_DIFFERENT` | non-equivalence proved |
| `UNKNOWN` | ran out of road — **not** the same as wrong |
| `UNPARSEABLE` | not valid input for this answer form |

Ask it something it cannot decide and it says so rather than guessing:

```python
>>> from mathbeast.verify import verify
>>> verify("1/0", "0")
CheckResult(verdict=<Verdict.UNKNOWN: 'unknown'>, expected='1/0', given='0',
            reason='no proof of equality or difference found')
```

`1/0` is undefined, so whether it equals zero is not a question the engine is
entitled to answer. It also refuses to guess the other way. A confident wrong
answer, and a confident *right* answer to an unanswerable question, are the same
failure — and a badge that cannot tell them apart is lying.

The parser is equally blunt about the near-misses. `g(a)` is rejected as an
undefined function rather than quietly read as `a*g`, and `x <= 3` is refused as
an expression because `x <= 3` and `x >= 3` share a boundary.

## Why the guarantee is narrower than the tagline

An LLM that "can't lie" would be false as written. Give a narrator a verified
answer and it can reach it by a method that never happened — the right number,
the wrong reasoning.

So narration is bound structurally, and checked without a model:

1. The narrator must emit exactly one line per verified step, in order, tagged
   with that step's id. It cannot invent a step or skip one.
2. Every mathematical claim in its prose must trace to that step's verified
   record — its expression before, its expression after, or its own step text.

A claim traceable to nothing is an **unsupported claim**, and it is reported.
That check is the file that makes the tagline honest, and it is also what
produces the benchmark number above.

## Answer forms

"What is the right answer" depends on what was asked. Getting this wrong is how
a tutor marks correct work as incorrect.

```python
>>> from mathbeast.forms import check, AnswerForm
>>> check("14.14213562", "14.1", AnswerForm.ROUNDED, "3sf").verdict
<Verdict.PROVEN_EQUAL: 'proven_equal'>          # over-precision is not an error
>>> check("14.14213562", "14.1", AnswerForm.EXACT).verdict
<Verdict.PROVEN_DIFFERENT: 'proven_different'>  # but exact really is exact
>>> check("2x = 6", "x = 3", AnswerForm.SET).verdict
<Verdict.PROVEN_EQUAL: 'proven_equal'>          # same solution, different route
```

Forms: `exact`, `rounded` (`3sf` / `2dp`), `set`, `interval`, `pair`.

## Coverage

C1 Number, C2 Algebra, C3 Geometry, C4 Mensuration, C5 Coordinate geometry,
C6 Trigonometry, C7–C8 Probability, C9 Statistics, E2 Algebra (Extended),
E4 Mensuration (Extended).

E1, E3 and E5 have no skills yet, and worded exam problems are not modelled
properly. [Full map, including what is missing](docs/syllabus-map.md).

> **Sub-codes are provisional.** Section codes (C1–C9, E1–E5) are verified and
> enforced in code; the codes below them (`C1.10`, `E2.3`) were reconstructed
> from public summaries rather than the official PDF. Checking one against the
> specification is a good first issue.

## Write a skill in twenty minutes

Skills are YAML. No Python, no SymPy, no executable code — which is why
good-first-issue PRs are safe to merge from strangers.

```yaml
id: 0580.c2.1.collect_terms
syllabus: C2.1
tier: core
title: Collecting like terms
statement: "Simplify {expr}."
display: "{a}{v} + {b}{v} + {c}"
answer: "{a}*{v} + {b}*{v} + {c}"
answer_form: exact
transform: collect
params:
  v: { dist: const, value: x }
  a: { dist: int, range: [2, 15] }
  b: { dist: int, range: [2, 15] }
  c: { dist: int, range: [-20, 20] }
steps:
  - "The x terms go together: {a} + {b} = {psum}."
```

Six gates apply automatically, including one that makes the engine's answer
verify against the project's own checker — if that fails, the claim "verified
by construction" is false, and that is where it surfaces.

→ [Full authoring guide](docs/authoring-skills.md) · [CONTRIBUTING](CONTRIBUTING.md)

## Prior art, and why this is still worth doing

The verified-engine pattern is not new, and the author of this repo would rather
say so than have a reader discover it:

- [noveoko/math_tutor](https://github.com/noveoko/math_tutor) — a verified
  adaptive tutoring engine with self-verifying generators and CAS judges. The
  closest existing thing to this project. 0 stars.
- [stellawuellner/math-worksheets-skill](https://github.com/stellawuellner/math-worksheets-skill)
  — an audited SymPy verifier with a pinned version floor, a strict allowlist
  parser and a weekly CAS canary. The best-executed version of this thesis, and
  the source of several decisions here.
- [openai/prm800k](https://github.com/openai/prm800k) — SymPy answer grading
  backing a paper. 2.1k stars.
- [lukew3/mathgenerator](https://github.com/lukew3/mathgenerator) — plain
  procedural generation, no verification. 738 stars, unmaintained.

The pattern existing is not the interesting part. The observation that
something like this can ship five times and still be at zero stars, while a
plain generator is at 738, is what this project is a bet on: **the engine is
commodity, the measurement is not.**

Everything is generated from templates written here, so this ships no past
papers and carries no copyright exposure.
